extractions.title: Weekend Edition.
key_claims: Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, one of seven Republican senators who voted to convict Trump in his 2021 impeachment trial, failed to make a runoff in his state primary.
Cassidy's loss is described as the most significant defeat for a Republican who sought to hold Trump accountable since Liz Cheney lost her primary in 2022.
Trump-endorsed candidate Rep. Julia Letlow advanced to a June 27 runoff with 45 percent of the vote, while Cassidy trailed with 24 percent.
Letlow will face John Fleming, the state treasurer, in the runoff after neither candidate won an outright majority.

Analyst Amy Walter framed upcoming elections as a battle between political environment factors (like inflation and the war in Iran) that help Democrats, and structural partisanship that helps Republicans.

extractions.title: Security Cannot Be Built on the Threat of Catastrophe
key_claims: Alyn Ware argues that lasting security cannot be built against others but must be built with them, through 'common security' rather than nuclear deterrence.
Nuclear-armed ships and submarines from the United States visited New Zealand ports as part of the ANZUS alliance, which Ware opposed on moral grounds.

Indigenous Pacific communities were treated as expendable during nuclear testing by France, the UK, and the United States, with Pacific islands used as testing grounds due to their distance from major powers' mainland territories.

A 1974 legal challenge by Australia and New Zealand against French nuclear testing at the International Court of Justice demonstrated that international institutions can influence the behavior of powerful states.

Ware has worked through the International Court of Justice, the United Nations, parliamentarians, and global civil society networks to advance nuclear disarmament through patient, incremental, and law-based approaches.

extractions.title: May 16, 2026
key_claims: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously decided Brown v. Board of Education, declaring racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Senator Strom Thurmond launched the longest filibuster in U.S. history at 24 hours and 18 minutes to block the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
Senator Cory Booker broke Thurmond's filibuster record on March 31–April 1, 2025, speaking for 25 hours, 5 minutes, and 59 seconds, though his speech was not a filibuster.
James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by KKK members working with local law enforcement and buried in an earthen dam under construction near Philadelphia, Mississippi.

In Selma, Alabama, the city's voting rolls were 99% white despite Black Americans outnumbering white Americans in a city of 29,500 people, and a judge banned public gatherings of more than two people to stop voter registration meetings.

extractions.title: I Blame My Father's Summer Reading Lists
key_claims: The author's life choices, including a 15,000-mile solo road trip across America at age 27, can be traced back to summer reading lists assigned by her father.

Her father, a professor of French and Francophone literature, gave her books far beyond her emotional comprehension, including Nabokov's Lolita at age twelve and works by Anaïs Nin, Paul Bowles, Fanon, and Camus.
Reading Isabelle Eberhardt's journals at fourteen profoundly shaped her relationship to the desert and her sense of restlessness and freedom.
Her father's biography 'The Immortal Journeys of Isabelle Eberhardt' was published the week the article was written.

The author later traced versions of Isabelle Eberhardt's journeys through North Africa, including study in Morocco's Atlas Mountains, oral history work in Tunisia, and excursions into the Sahara, Sinai, and Wadi Rum.
